title: Internal Consistency as a Faithfulness Proxy: Do CoT Claims Predict Final Answer Logic?

original_idea.quick_reasoning: Clearly addresses an AI Safety problem with a reasonably scoped approach.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Downgraded. The NLI-as-faithfulness-proxy approach has already been published (EMNLP Findings 2024) and the field has moved to more sophisticated methods. Marginal incremental contribution.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Using an NLI model to check entailment between CoT steps and final answers is well-documented. Running 500 model outputs through an NLI pipeline is standard. Accessible to beginners with medium compute.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Clear single experiment: run NLI on CoT-answer pairs, compute consistency rates across model families and tasks. One deliverable: consistency rate comparison table. Achievable in 30 hours.

novelty.reasoning: This space is heavily explored in 2024-2025. 'Measuring and Improving Faithfulness of Chain-of-Thought Reasoning' (EMNLP Findings 2024) directly uses NLI-based consistency checking and reports it has statistically significant capability in detecting factual and causal issues in CoT. 'Measuring Chain of Thought Faithfulness by Unlearning Reasoning Steps' (EMNLP 2025, arXiv:2502.14829) provides a more principled approach to faithfulness measurement. 'Measuring Chain-of-Thought Monitorability Through Faithfulness and Verbosity' (arXiv:2510.27378, 2025) proposes monitorability as a practical alternative. 'On the Hardness of Faithful Chain-of-Thought Reasoning' (2024) establishes theoretical limitations. The specific NLI-as-proxy approach is directly addressed by existing EMNLP 2024 work, and the broader space has moved beyond this to more sophisticated methods.
